alternatives: No cache (deactivation is always immediate)
Per-app cache with a short TTL, invalidated on DELETE in the same process; stale for up to the TTL on other workers or replicas

alternatives: Modest: up to about 50 RPS, p95 < 100 ms, best effort (one instance is enough)
Medium: about 500 RPS, p95 < 100 ms, 99.9% availability (needs PostgreSQL and several workers)
Large: several thousand RPS or TV-spike bursts (needs PostgreSQL, multiple replicas, possibly an edge cache and an asynchronous click pipeline)
data.rationale: The target decides the architecture. Modest load can be met with the WAL/pool/lean-query changes in this spec. Medium load requires a PostgreSQL deployment and driver. Large load needs caching and asynchronous click ingestion, which conflict with immediate deactivation and synchronous counts and cannot be delivered safely in one week.

If production is PostgreSQL or MySQL, we must add and pin a driver, validate the pool defaults for it, and FR-19's collation fix becomes urgent. alternatives: Formatted 'PRAGMA busy_timeout=%d' (rejected: SQL string formatting is banned by policy)
Move production to PostgreSQL now (rejected by Q-2: no new driver; documented only)
Keep rollback-journal mode and only shorten busy_timeout (rejected: lookups would still block behind writers)
data.rationale: For file-based SQLite URLs, create_db_engine registers a 'connect' event listener that calls apply_sqlite_pragmas(dbapi_connection). That function runs the literal statements 'PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL' and 'PRAGMA synchronous=NORMAL' on a DBAPI cursor and tolerates failure: it logs a WARNING and continues in the existing journal mode. busy_timeout is set by passing connect_args={'check_same_thread': False, 'timeout': (SQLITE_BUSY_TIMEOUT_MS + 0.5) / 1000}. CPython computes sqlite3_busy_timeout as (int)(timeout*1000), so the +0.5 makes PRAGMA busy_timeout report exactly SQLITE_BUSY_TIMEOUT_MS with no float truncation. The default of 5000 equals today's pysqlite default. — With WAL, readers never block behind the click and create writers, so the redirect lookup is not stalled. synchronous=NORMAL removes the fsync per commit in WAL mode, which is safe against corruption; at most the last transactions can be lost on power failure, which is acceptable for best effort. Setting busy_timeout through the connect arg avoids building a PRAGMA with string formatting, which is banned by policy. The connect event applies to every pooled connection, and WAL persists in the file, so the deployed database upgrades automatically with no manual step.
data.title: ADR-1: Harden SQLite at the engine level: WAL and synchronous=NORMAL through a connect event, busy_timeout through the pysqlite timeout connect arg

alternatives: Force QueuePool for all URLs (breaks in-memory semantics)
NullPool for SQLite (connect cost per request; pragmas re-run on every request)
data.rationale: Pass pool_size, max_overflow and pool_timeout to create_engine for file-based SQLite (SQLAlchemy 2.0 uses QueuePool there) and for non-SQLite URLs. Do not pass them for in-memory SQLite ('sqlite://', ':memory:', 'mode=memory', 'file::memory:'), which uses SingletonThreadPool and would reject max_overflow and pool_timeout. — This meets FR-16 and the defaults (5/10/30) reproduce current behaviour. In-memory URLs used in tests keep working.
data.title: ADR-2: Configurable pool only where a QueuePool exists

alternatives: api_route(methods=['GET','HEAD']) (adds head operations to OpenAPI and emits duplicate operation-id warnings)
Excluding reserved codes inside redirect_head (couples the redirect to probe knowledge; the 404 semantics would still be wrong)
data.rationale: Add @router.head('/healthz', include_in_schema=False) and @router.head('/readyz', include_in_schema=False), each returning an empty Response(200). The GET routes are unchanged. Readiness logic is shared through a private _check_ready(db) helper. — The health router is included before the redirect router, so HEAD /healthz and HEAD /readyz become FULL matches before HEAD /{code}. The OpenAPI document stays identical: there is no new 'head' operation and no duplicate-operationId warning, which api_route(methods=['GET','HEAD']) would cause. POST still produces a 405 because the path matches only partially.
data.title: ADR-3: HEAD probes as dedicated hidden routes on the health router

alternatives: Stream timestamps with yield_per and bucket in Python (O(1) memory but O(clicks) time)
func.date everywhere (PostgreSQL date() semantics are less explicit; CAST is clearer)
SQL ORDER BY plus LIMIT 10 for referrers (collation-dependent tie order; NULL ordering differs by dialect)
data.rationale: click_repository defines class UtcDate(FunctionElement) with type=Date() and inherit_cache=True, compiled with sqlalchemy.ext.compiler.compiles. The default (PostgreSQL and others) compiles to CAST(x AS DATE); sqlite and mysql/mariadb compile to date(x) / DATE(x). The compiler functions delegate to compiler.process(cast(...)) and compiler.process(func.date(...)), so no SQL string formatting is needed. The query is GROUP BY day ORDER BY day for one link_id with created_at >= since. Referrer counts keep GROUP BY on the raw column; '' and NULL are merged in Python, and the service still sorts and caps at 10. — Stored timestamps are naive UTC, so a date cast with no timezone conversion gives exact UTC-day bucketing on all three dialects. Memory is O(days + referrer groups) (NFR-13). The construct compiles for all dialects without a driver, which makes the FR-18 compile test straightforward. Keeping the Python sort for referrers preserves the exact ordering semantics, including NULL last, independent of database collation. Grouping on the raw column avoids the PostgreSQL GROUP BY bound-parameter mismatch that nullif(referrer, :p) would cause.
data.title: ADR-4: Stats daily buckets aggregated in SQL through a dialect-compiled UtcDate construct

alternatives: Per-app TTL cache (stale 307 after takedown; NFR-9 static rule)
Background or batched click writes (changes the visibility contract; possible click loss)
data.rationale: LinkRepository.get_redirect_target(code) runs select(Link.id, Link.url, Link.is_active).where(Link.code == code) and returns RedirectTarget(id, url, is_active) or None. Redirect resolution uses it. Deactivation, detail and stats keep get_by_code. There is no redirect cache and no async click ingestion. — This gives the minimum hot-path SQL (FR-17) with no ORM identity-map or refresh overhead. Without a cache, the 410 after deactivation stays immediate (FR-7, Q-4), and synchronous clicks keep counts visible at once (Q-5). The 50 RPS target is met without either.
data.title: ADR-5: Narrow redirect lookup returning a NamedTuple, with no cache

alternatives: Keep logger.exception at ERROR (traceback text includes SQL parameters; noisier under contention)
data.rationale: In resolve_and_record_click, any exception from the click add or commit is followed by session.rollback() (its own failure is suppressed) and exactly one logger.warning('failed to record click for link_id=%s error=%s', link_id, type(exc).__name__) on 'app.services.links'. There is no traceback and no exception message. The 307 is still returned. — FR-15 requires exactly one warning line without the IP, and NFR-14 forbids leaking request data. DBAPI exception text can contain bound parameters (referrer, user agent, hash), so logging only the class name is safe and still countable for the lost-clicks metric.
data.title: ADR-6: Click-failure logging at WARNING without exc_info

alternatives: sqlalchemy.dialects.mysql.VARCHAR(collation=...) (violates test_orm_uses_declarative_base_and_portable_types)
An automatic migration (no migration tooling; out of scope)
data.rationale: Link.code = mapped_column(String(32).with_variant(String(32, collation='utf8mb4_bin'), 'mysql', 'mariadb'), nullable=False). The docs give the manual ALTER TABLE for existing MySQL databases. — type(col.type) stays sqltypes.String and the module does not import sqlalchemy.dialects, so the existing portability test passes. DDL for SQLite and PostgreSQL is unchanged (NFR-18).
data.title: ADR-7: MySQL case-sensitive codes through a portable type variant

alternatives: Log the settings object (risk of leaking DATABASE_URL credentials and API_KEY)
data.rationale: core/db.py provides describe_db_tuning(engine, settings) -> dict and format_db_tuning(dict) -> str. In the lifespan after create_all, main.py logs on 'app.db' at INFO: message 'database tuning ' + format_db_tuning(tuning), with extra={'db_tuning': tuning}. 'db_tuning' is added to the JsonFormatter extra fields. — Operators can confirm the campaign configuration from the logs (NFR-16/NFR-20). The URL is never included, so credentials cannot leak (NFR-15). PRAGMA values are read back from a real pooled connection, so they reflect the effective settings.
data.title: ADR-8: Startup tuning log line built from the engine and settings, without the URL

alternatives: PRAGMA busy_timeout=<n> built with formatting (violates policy)
Move to PostgreSQL now (rejected by Q-2; needs a driver)
Leave the rollback journal and only add a busy timeout (readers would still block)
data.rationale:
For file-based SQLite:
- create_engine(url, poolclass=QueuePool, pool_size, max_overflow, pool_timeout, connect_args={'check_same_thread': False, 'timeout': (SQLITE_BUSY_TIMEOUT_MS + 0.5) / 1000.0}).
- An event.listens_for(engine, 'connect') handler executes the literal statements 'PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL' and 'PRAGMA synchronous=NORMAL' on a raw DBAPI cursor.
- The +0.5 ms makes pysqlite's int(timeout*1000) truncation land exactly on the configured value.

In-memory SQLite gets only check_same_thread=False. Non-SQLite gets pool_pre_ping=True plus the pool settings. — WAL lets readers proceed while a writer holds the lock, which is what stops redirects queueing behind creates and clicks. The sqlite3 timeout parameter installs the busy handler without building a PRAGMA string, so the literal-only SQL policy holds. QueuePool kwargs are not valid for SingletonThreadPool/StaticPool, so in-memory URLs skip them.
data.title: ADR-1: Harden SQLite with a connect listener, connect_args timeout and QueuePool settings

alternatives: Alembic migrations (out of scope)
Documented manual ALTER only (operator error risk RK-11)
A separate link_expiry table (more joins on the hot path)
data.rationale:
After create_all, the lifespan calls app.core.schema.ensure_links_expires_at(engine):
- It uses sqlalchemy.inspect on a fresh connection.
- If 'expires_at' is not among the links columns, it runs the dialect-guarded literal ALTER inside engine.begin().
- It logs 'added' or 'already_present'.
- On any exception it logs an ERROR and re-raises, so startup aborts. — There is one additive, nullable column and a one-week deadline. Alembic would add a dependency, a workflow and operator steps. Without the upgrade, every redirect on the deployed DB would return 503. Failing startup loudly is better than serving 503s.
data.title: ADR-2: Idempotent startup ALTER instead of migration tooling

alternatives: WHERE expires_at > :now in SQL (cannot distinguish 404, 410-deactivated and 410-expired without a second query)
In-process cache of links (forbidden; breaks immediate deactivation and expiry)
data.rationale: LinkRepository.get_redirect_target selects only id, url, is_active and expires_at. LinkService._check_redirectable(target) raises GoneError() if the link is inactive, then GoneError(LINK_EXPIRED_DETAIL) if expires_at is not None and self._utcnow() >= expires_at. GET and HEAD both go through _resolve_target, which calls _check_redirectable. The clock is LinkService(now=callable|None); _utcnow() calls it, falling back to models.utcnow(), and normalises to naive UTC. — This adds no SQL statements (FR-17). The rule is evaluated on every request with no cache (FR-22), and both methods share one helper (RK-14). Deactivation takes precedence. Tests are deterministic.
data.title: ADR-3: Expiry evaluated in Python on the narrow lookup row, with an injectable clock

alternatives: Always hash a JSON payload (breaks old keys, RK-15)
Ignore expires_at in the hash (silent replay of a different payload)
data.rationale: request_hash = sha256(url) when expires_at is None; otherwise sha256(url + '\n' + canonical UTC instant 'YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS.ffffffZ'). The replay check runs before the future-instant check. — Keys stored before the deploy (url-only hashes) keep replaying. The same instant written with different offsets hashes identically. Adding or changing expires_at gives 409. Replays return the stored link even after the expiry has passed, which matches how deactivated links replay.
data.title: ADR-4: Backward-compatible idempotency hash

alternatives: Stream timestamps with yield_per and bucket in Python (portable but O(clicks) time)
Denormalised hourly counter table (new schema, out of scope)
data.rationale:
Daily and hourly stats use SELECT bucket, COUNT(id) ... WHERE link_id = :id AND created_at >= :start [AND created_at < :end] GROUP BY bucket.

Day bucket:
- sqlite: func.date(created_at)
- postgresql (and the fallback): cast(created_at, Date)
- mysql/mariadb: func.date(created_at)

Hour bucket:
- sqlite: func.strftime(literal_column("'%Y-%m-%d %H:00:00'"), created_at)
- postgresql (and the fallback): func.date_trunc(literal_column("'hour'"), created_at)
- mysql/mariadb: func.timestampadd(literal_column('HOUR'), func.hour(created_at), func.date(created_at))

Result values are normalised in Python (str -> date/datetime). Module-level statement builders take dialect_name so tests can compile them for all three dialects. — Memory is O(days) or O(hours) and the query uses the covering (link_id, created_at) index. With no bind parameters inside the bucket expression, the GROUP BY matches the SELECT expression on PostgreSQL. String formats are constants, not SQL formatting.
data.title: ADR-5: SQL aggregation with dialect-guarded bucket expressions that use no bound parameters

alternatives: api_route(methods=['GET','HEAD']) (adds 'head' operations to the OpenAPI schema and relies on the server to strip the body)
data.rationale: health.py adds @router.head('/healthz', include_in_schema=False) and @router.head('/readyz', include_in_schema=False). They return Response(status_code=200) with an empty body. /readyz shares a private _check_database(db) helper with GET. — This guarantees an empty body and leaves the OpenAPI path and operation set untouched. The health router is included before the catch-all, so HEAD /{code} never sees these paths. POST still yields 405.
data.title: ADR-6: Explicit HEAD routes for the probes

alternatives: session.commit() after the read (shows up as a second COMMIT in the query budget)
BEGIN IMMEDIATE for the whole redirect (serialises reads behind writers)
Asynchronous click ingestion (out of scope, Q-5)
data.rationale:
In resolve_and_record_click, after the lookup and checks, call self.session.rollback(). This ends the read transaction and is a transaction-boundary call, not a statement. Then call ClickRepository.add(...) and session.commit() inside try/except Exception. On failure:
- Roll back, suppressing any secondary exception.
- Log exactly one logger.warning('failed to record click for link_id=%s (%s)', link_id, type(exc).__name__), with no IP, no exception message and no traceback.
- Return the URL. — This avoids SQLITE_BUSY_SNAPSHOT on the read-to-write upgrade under WAL and bounds the added latency to the busy timeout. The exception message can contain bound SQL parameters, so it is not logged. ClickRepository.add remains the patch point used by existing tests.
data.title: ADR-7: End the read transaction before the click insert; best-effort WARNING on failure

alternatives: Pydantic validator calling datetime.now() (cannot be tested deterministically; would break replay)
Raise HTTPException from the services (violates layering)
data.rationale: Add InvalidInputError(AppError) with status 422 in app/core/errors.py. Schemas only parse and normalise (to naive UTC, non-string values rejected). LinkService raises InvalidInputError('expires_at must be in the future') using its injectable clock. StatsService raises InvalidInputError for invalid hourly ranges. — Validation that depends on the clock must use the injectable clock and must be skipped on idempotent replay. A Pydantic validator cannot do either. The error body stays {"detail": "..."}.
data.title: ADR-8: Future-instant validation in the service with a 422 domain error

alternatives: Add no-store to every AppError in the global handler (wider blast radius)
data.rationale: redirect.py catches NotFoundError and GoneError from the service and returns JSONResponse({'detail': exc.detail}, status_code=exc.status_code, headers={'Cache-Control': 'no-store'}). Other exceptions propagate to the global handlers (SQLAlchemyError -> 503). — Browsers and CDNs could otherwise cache a 410 or 404 after a link is created, cleared or extended. Expiry and PATCH changes take effect immediately (NFR-15).
data.title: ADR-9: No-store on redirect-path error responses

alternatives: A global collation (breaks SQLite)
Dialect-specific types from sqlalchemy.dialects (forbidden in models)
data.rationale: Declare code as String(32).with_variant(String(32, collation='utf8mb4_bin'), 'mysql', 'mariadb'). Document the manual DDL for existing MySQL databases: ALTER TABLE links MODIFY code VARCHAR(32) CHARACTER SET utf8mb4 COLLATE utf8mb4_bin NOT NULL; — This keeps portable sqltypes (type(col.type) is still sqltypes.String) and leaves the SQLite and PostgreSQL DDL unchanged.
data.title: ADR-10: MySQL case-sensitive codes via a type variant
